title: The Russian join
subtitle: How to join two yarn ends by threading each tail back through its own strand
excerpt: The Russian join creates a looped join between two yarn ends by weaving each tail back through itself. It holds on slippery yarns where a knot would slip and leaves no tails to weave in.
sourceNotes: Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book.

glossaryTerms.definition: A yarn-joining method that loops each yarn tail back through its own strand using the tapestry needle, creating an interlocked loop join that holds without knots.
The loose end of yarn left after cutting at a fastened-off point or at a join.

content.text: by weaving each one back through its own strand with the needle, then hooking the loops together. It works well on slippery fibres (silk, superwash wool, linen) where a magic knot would slip. No tails need weaving in after.
Thread the end of the old yarn onto the tapestry needle. Leave about 12 cm of tail.
Fold the tail back on itself to form a loop. Thread the needle back through the plies of the old yarn strand (not just around it) for about 3 cm, working toward the folded end.
Pull through, leaving the loop at the end.
Thread the new yarn through the loop of the old yarn end.
Repeat steps 2 and 3 with the new yarn end, threading it back through itself with the loop passing through the old yarn's loop.
Pull both working strands gently in opposite directions. The two interlocked loops slide together.
Trim the tails close to the join. There are no loose ends remaining.
The trade-off versus the magic knot

The Russian join takes longer to work than the magic knot. It also creates a slightly thicker point where both strands are doubled back through themselves. On dense fabric this is invisible; on lace or fine work it may show. The magic knot is faster; the Russian join is more reliable on slippery fibres.

items.symptom: The needle splits the plies unevenly and the yarn shreds
items.cause: The tapestry needle is too sharp or too large for the yarn.
items.fix: Use a blunt tapestry needle that parts the plies rather than cutting through them. For very fine yarn, the tapestry needle that is slightly smaller than the yarn diameter works best.

items.symptom: The join creates a visible lump on fine yarn
items.cause: The doubled section of each strand is too long.
items.fix: Thread back through the plies for only 2 cm rather than 3 cm. A shorter folded section creates a smaller, less visible join.

content.text: Practice the Russian join on a short length of yarn before using it on a project. The step of threading the needle back through the plies of its own strand takes one or two tries to get the angle right. Once it is familiar it takes under two minutes per join.
